hints: Notice that white phosphorus exists as P4 molecules, not single P atoms, so the molar mass is what matters here.
Calculate the Mr of P4 using Ar of P = 31, then find moles in 62 g with moles = mass divided by Mr.
Convert your moles of P4 into molecules using L, remembering one mole always contains L particles.
walkthrough:
**Find the molar mass of P4**

White phosphorus is made of P4 molecules. Each P atom has Ar = 31.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$M_r(\text{P}_4) = 4 \times 31 = 124 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$$

**Calculate moles of P4 in 62 g**

Use the friendly mole formula, moles equals mass over Mr. 62 g is exactly half of 124 g.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{moles} = \frac{\text{mass}}{M_r} = \frac{62}{124} = 0.5 \text{ mol}$$

**Convert moles to number of molecules**

One mole of anything contains L particles, where L is the Avogadro constant. So half a mole contains half of L.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{number of molecules} = 0.5 \times L = \frac{L}{2}$$

options.A: This would mean 1 mole of P4 is present. That would need 124 g of P4, not 62 g. It comes from forgetting to multiply Ar by 4 and treating 62 g as one mole.
options.B: This is the number of phosphorus ATOMS, not molecules. Since 62/31 = 2 mol of P atoms, you get 2L atoms. But those atoms are grouped in fours as P4, so molecules are four times fewer.
options.C: Correct and well done. 62 g is 0.5 mol of P4 molecules (62/124), and 0.5 mol contains 0.5 x L = L/2 molecules.
options.D: This is too small by a factor of 2. It comes from finding 0.5 mol correctly but then dividing by 4 again. You only divide by 4 once when you use Mr = 124, no extra division is needed.
